Stochastic Weight Averaging (SWA) collects model snapshots along the SGD trajectory and averages their weights, exploiting the geometry of loss basins where flat regions tend to produce better-generalizing solutions than sharp minima. The central question here is whether the shape of the learning rate schedule — not just its final value or cycle length — systematically biases which part of the loss landscape gets explored, and therefore which points get averaged together. A cosine anneal pulls the iterate toward a basin center before the next cycle kicks it out again, while a constant-then-drop schedule leaves the iterate wandering a wider region; the average of these two exploration patterns will land in geometrically different places even if the loss values look similar. The key concepts to hold simultaneously are: the ergodicity of the SGD trajectory under a given schedule (does it thoroughly sample a basin or hug one wall?), the curvature structure of the averaging manifold (the straight-line average of two low-loss points may pass through high-loss territory if the basin is non-convex), and the interaction between cycle frequency and the correlation length of weight updates.

What a beginner misses is that "more averaging is better" is only true if the averaged iterates are roughly exchangeable samples from the same flat basin — if the schedule shape causes iterates from different basins to be collected, the average can land in a high-loss ridge between them, and the resulting model is worse than any individual snapshot. An expert also worries about the implicit momentum bias: schedules with long high-LR phases bias collected weights toward regions of high gradient noise, which may not coincide with the flat minima that make SWA work in the first place.

Entezari et al. The property that makes SWA's average safe — and that a naive cross-run average lacks — is that consecutive cycle endpoints are continuously deformed versions of each other, so they lie in the same symmetry-equivalence class and their midpoint stays in the same basin. What breaks down is when the learning rate is high enough, or the cycle long enough, that an iterate effectively escapes to a new symmetry class — at that point the averaged weights can degrade badly even though both endpoints look fine individually.

Gradient checkpointing does not alter the computational graph — it only changes which activations are stored versus recomputed, leaving the forward and backward pass mathematically identical — so it poses no threat to symmetry equivalence. Stochastic depth is the genuinely dangerous case: when layers are randomly dropped during training (Huang et al., 2016, with drop rates up to 0.5 on late ResNet layers), each forward pass effectively samples a different sub-architecture, meaning the loss surface the optimizer walks on is itself a mixture over sub-graphs, not a fixed manifold. The permutation-equivalence argument for LMC was derived for fixed architectures; when the active subnetwork changes cycle-to-cycle, two iterates may have their low-loss structure "stored" in overlapping but non-identical layer subsets, and the straight-line average mixes weight scales from layers that were active at different rates — a form of implicit misalignment even without crossing basins. Empirically you would detect breakage by computing the loss barrier profile: interpolate α·w₁ + (1-α)·w₂ for α ∈ {0, 0.1, …, 1.0} with stochastic depth disabled at evaluation time, and measure the maximum loss elevation at the midpoint relative to the endpoints; a barrier above ~1% test error degradation on something like CIFAR-100 with a WideResNet signals that symmetry equivalence has been compromised. A cleaner diagnostic is to compare the CKA (centered kernel alignment) similarity of intermediate representations between the two endpoint networks: if stochastic depth has driven them into genuinely different functional organizations, CKA scores at middle layers will drop markedly below the ~0.95+ values you'd expect from same-run SWA endpoints. The practical fix used implicitly in networks like EfficientNet and Stochastic Depth ResNets is to anneal the drop rate toward zero in the final SWA collection phase, restoring a fixed computational graph precisely when the averaging snapshots are being gathered.

The generalization benefit of stochastic depth is largely front-loaded: it acts as a regularizer during the loss-basin-shaping phase of training, steering the optimizer toward flatter, more robust regions, and by the time you enter the SWA collection window the basin geometry is already set. The more precise concern is whether late-phase stochastic depth was actively maintaining flatness through gradient noise, versus merely having already shaped the basin earlier — and Izmailov et al.'s original SWA paper (2018) is actually instructive here: SWA works best when the pre-SWA training has already found a good basin, and the collection phase just needs a stable, low-noise trajectory to average within it, suggesting the regularizer's structural job is done. However, there is a real but underappreciated risk: if your base learning rate during SWA collection is high enough that the iterate is still exploring basin walls, removing stochastic depth simultaneously sharpens the effective loss surface and reduces gradient noise, potentially causing the trajectory to converge to a sharper sub-region of the basin than it would have with stochastic depth retained at a low residual rate (say 0.1 rather than full 0.5). The practical evidence from EfficientNet-style training (Tan & Le, 2019) suggests a compromise works well: anneal stochastic depth to a small nonzero value (~0.1) rather than fully to zero, preserving enough graph stochasticity to keep gradient noise high without introducing severe layer-scale misalignment between averaged snapshots. The diagnostic is straightforward — compute the Hessian trace or sharpness (∂²L/∂w² approximated via Hutchinson's estimator) of the SWA average under full-anneal versus partial-anneal conditions; if full anneal produces a noticeably higher trace, you've confirmed the basin has sharpened and the SWA average will generalize worse despite looking fine on training loss.

Uniform averaging does not minimize sharpness in general — it minimizes the Euclidean distance from the average to the centroid of the snapshot cloud, which is a geometric property with no direct relationship to the Hessian structure of the loss at that centroid. The sharpness of a weight average is determined by the curvature at the averaged point, not the average of curvatures at the individual snapshots, so upweighting flat iterates only helps if flatness is spatially correlated in a way that pulls the centroid toward flatter sub-regions — a nontrivial assumption that depends on basin geometry. Cha et al. (2021, SWAD — "Domain Generalization by Seeking Flat Minima") tested exactly this idea in the domain generalization setting: they used a loss-based density weighting scheme that oversampled iterates near the loss floor, and found ~1-2% accuracy gains on DomainBed benchmarks over uniform SWA, confirming that the snapshot distribution shape matters. The mechanism SWAD exploits is that the loss floor of a basin is often spatially correlated with lower sharpness (flat basins tend to be flat throughout, not just at one point), so loss-weighted averaging acts as a proxy for sharpness-weighted averaging without requiring expensive Hessian computation. A pure sharpness-aware weighting scheme would require estimating the Hessian trace at each snapshot — via Hutchinson's estimator this costs roughly 10-20 additional forward-backward passes per snapshot — and Andriushchenko & Flammarion (2022) showed in the SAM literature that sharpness estimates at individual iterates are noisy enough that the ranking of snapshots by sharpness is unreliable without averaging over multiple perturbation directions, making the compute cost potentially prohibitive. The deeper issue is that for non-convex basins, the average of flat points can land on a ridge between them, so sharpness-weighted averaging is only guaranteed to help when the flat iterates are co-located in weight space — a condition you should verify empirically by checking whether sharpness and L2 distance from the centroid are negatively correlated in your specific model.

The confound is real and precise: at the cosine cycle trough, SGD's effective noise scale is η·σ² where η→0, so the iterate is essentially frozen and its mini-batch gradient norm reflects optimizer stillness rather than landscape flatness — a sharp minimum looks identical to a flat one under this metric. The cleanest fix is to measure gradient norm at a fixed reference learning rate, decoupled from the current schedule: after collecting a snapshot, evaluate the gradient norm using a held-out batch with a standardized perturbation scale ε (e.g., ε = 0.01·‖w‖), which removes the η dependence entirely and measures intrinsic landscape slope. A cheaper and more elegant approach is the loss sharpness ratio: compute L(w + δ) − L(w) where δ is a random unit-norm perturbation scaled to a fixed ε, averaged over ~5 perturbation directions — this is schedule-agnostic by construction, costs 5 extra forward passes, and is essentially the Hutchinson diagonal estimator restricted to random directions. Keskar et al. (2017) used exactly this perturbation-based sharpness measure (their C-sharpness metric) and showed it distinguished sharp from flat minima reliably across batch sizes, precisely because it doesn't depend on the gradient magnitude at the point itself but on how quickly the loss rises when you leave the point. Empirically, the signature of a stillpoint-vs-genuine-flat confusion is a high variance in perturbation loss across directions at cycle troughs: a genuine flat minimum has uniformly low perturbation loss in all directions, while a sharp stillpoint has low gradient norm but high and anisotropic perturbation loss, so the coefficient of variation across perturbation directions is a direct diagnostic. The practical recommendation is to use perturbation-based sharpness rather than gradient norm for snapshot weighting whenever cosine or other decaying schedules are used, accepting the 5-10x forward pass overhead as the cost of schedule-invariant flatness estimation.

ε-scaling by ‖w‖ does not correctly normalize sharpness across snapshots with different weight norms — it introduces a systematic bias, but the direction depends on the network's homogeneity structure. For ReLU networks with weight normalization or BatchNorm, the loss is approximately scale-invariant: L(αw) ≈ L(w) for scalar α, which means the effective curvature in the loss landscape is invariant to ‖w‖, but the perturbation radius ε·‖w‖ grows with weight norm, so late-training snapshots with larger ‖w‖ get probed at a physically larger radius — artificially making them appear flatter than early snapshots with identical intrinsic curvature. The correct normalization for scale-invariant networks is to perturb in the manifold-tangent direction rather than Euclidean weight space: Dinh et al. (2017, "Sharp Minima Can Generalize For Deep Nets") showed explicitly that sharpness measures in Euclidean weight space are not invariant to reparameterization, and that any meaningful flatness measure must account for the network's symmetry group — for BatchNorm networks this means normalizing each layer's perturbation by that layer's weight norm separately, not the global ‖w‖. SAM's original implementation (Foret et al., 2021) uses exactly ε/‖∇L‖ · ∇L as the perturbation direction rather than a random direction scaled by ‖w‖, which partially addresses this by normalizing to gradient magnitude rather than weight magnitude — but this reintroduces the schedule-dependence problem we started with, since gradient magnitude is again confounded by learning rate. The empirically cleanest approach, used in Fisher-Rao normalization work (Liang et al., 2019), is to measure sharpness in Fisher information metric space rather than Euclidean weight space: the Fisher metric is reparameterization-invariant by construction, so snapshots with different weight norms are compared on equal footing, though computing even a diagonal Fisher approximation adds ~2-3x overhead versus raw perturbation sharpness. Practically, for SWA snapshot weighting the most defensible cheap fix is per-layer ε scaling — set εₗ = ε·‖wₗ‖ independently for each layer — which handles the dominant source of scale non-invariance (BatchNorm weight drift) without requiring Fisher computation, and is what modern SAM variants like GSAM and mSAM implicitly approximate.
